All 30 conformers share the same connectivity: a pentan-2-ol backbone (CH3-CH2-CH2-CH(-)-CH2OH) in which the CH carbon (C6) also bears an aziridin-1-yl nitrogen (N7 bonded to two ring CH2 groups, C8/C9, that are also bonded to each other, forming the strained 3-membered aziridine ring). Since the aziridine ring geometry, bond lengths and overall connectivity are essentially invariant across conformers, the dominant conformation-dependent stabilizing interaction is the possible intramolecular hydrogen bond between the hydroxyl proton (H16 on O15) and the aziridine nitrogen lone pair (N7), which would close a favorable 5-membered pseudo-ring (O-C14-C6-N7...H). I measured the H16···N7 distance in every conformer as a direct proxy for this interaction (all such H-bonds show a similar, ring-constrained O-H···N angle of ~110-120°, so distance is a consistent measure of H-bond quality across the set).

Results split clearly into two groups: (1) conformers with H16···N7 distances of ~2.17-2.65 Å, consistent with a genuine (if somewhat bent, ring-constrained) intramolecular O-H···N hydrogen bond, and (2) conformers with H16···N7 distances of ~3.85-4.0 Å, where the hydroxyl is rotated/positioned away from the nitrogen and no such stabilization is possible. The H-bonded group should be substantially more stable due to the extra electrostatic/H-bond stabilization, and within that group shorter, more linear-ish contacts (lower distance) indicate a stronger, better-aligned interaction. Within the non-H-bonded group, stabilization differences are subtler (residual gauche/steric effects in the propyl chain and around C6), so ranking there is less certain and based on the small residual variation in the same distance metric plus general absence of severe steric clashes noted in a quick visual check of close contacts.

Based on this analysis, conformer 28 has the shortest, best-aligned O-H···N contact (2.17 Å) and is ranked most stable; conformers 6, 11, 25, 26 follow closely with strong H-bonds (~2.2 Å). Conformers 19, 3, 21, 17, 20, 24 have slightly longer but still clearly hydrogen-bonded geometries (2.26-2.30 Å). Conformers 14, 2, 27 (2.35-2.36 Å) and 8, 5, 9, 10, 7, 30, 16, 1 (2.5-2.65 Å) show progressively weaker/more distorted H-bonds. The remaining conformers (29, 4, 22, 23, 12, 15, 18, 13) show no meaningful O-H···N interaction (distances 3.8-4.0 Å) and are therefore judged least stable, ordered by the residual (non-bonding-range) distance as a weak tiebreaker since no stronger discriminating feature was evident from the coordinates.

Uncertainty: the exact ordering within the strongly H-bonded cluster (differences of only 0.01-0.05 Å) and within the non-H-bonded cluster is not highly reliable since it is based on a small geometric proxy without energy calculations; true energetic ordering could shuffle adjacent entries, especially where distances differ by <0.05 Å (e.g., 6 vs 11, or 16 vs 1).

The molecule is H2N-C(=O)-CH(C≡N)-NH-CH2-CH3 (an alpha-cyanoacetamide with an N-ethylamino substituent). Its conformational energy is dominated by whether an intramolecular H-bond forms between a donor N-H (either the secondary amine N-H, H4, or one of the primary-amide N-H's, H12/H13) and an acceptor (the carbonyl O10, the nitrile N7, or the amine N3 lone pair), each of which can close a favorable 5- or 6-membered ring. I computed, for every conformer, the through-space distances for the candidate H-bonds: (a) H4···O10 (5-membered ring via N3-C5-C9-O10), (b) H4···N7 (5-membered ring via N3-C5-C6-N7), (c) H12/H13···N7 (6-membered ring via N11-C9-C5-C6-N7), and (d) H12/H13···N3 (5-membered ring via N11-C9-C5-N3). The shortest of these contacts (generally in the 2.1-2.5 Å range when a real H-bond is present, versus 3-5 Å when no intramolecular H-bond is available) was used as the principal stability descriptor, since a well-formed N-H···O or N-H···N intramolecular contact in this small, flexible, polar molecule provides the largest differential stabilization (worth several kcal/mol) compared with subtler steric/eclipsing effects, which are harder to quantify reliably from a single static geometry.

Conformers with the shortest H-bonding contacts (≈2.10-2.20 Å, typically the amide N-H···amine-N (5-ring) or amine N-H···carbonyl-O (5-ring) motif nicely closed) were ranked as most stable: 26, 3, 11, 20, 14, 29, 13, 8, 19, 6, 10. A middle group (17, 18, 27, 12, 25, 5, 9, 30, 4, 23) shows moderate H-bond distances (2.2-2.35 Å), still stabilizing but somewhat less optimally geometered (donor/acceptor slightly misaligned or ring slightly strained). A further group (15, 16, 1, 2, 22) shows weak/long contacts (2.4-2.5 Å), indicating a poorly formed or nearly broken intramolecular H-bond, leaving the molecule more exposed to solvent-independent (gas-phase) destabilization. The least stable conformers (7, 21, 24, 28) have no close intramolecular H-bond candidate below ~2.7 Å for any of the four motifs, meaning the polar N-H and carbonyl/nitrile groups are not engaged intramolecularly at all, leaving these structures with the least internal stabilization and presumably higher relative energy (extended/open conformations of the ethylamino and amide arms).

Uncertainty: distances within ~0.05 Å of each other (e.g., 26/3/11 all ≈2.11 Å, or 8/19/6/10 all ≈2.17-2.20 Å) are essentially indistinguishable by this simple geometric proxy and their exact order could easily invert with a proper QM energy evaluation; likewise, steric/eclipsing contributions from the ethyl and CH2CN/amide rotamers were not separately quantified and could shift the ranking within each cluster. The overall grouping (strong H-bond > moderate > weak > none) is the most confident part of this analysis.

The molecule in all 30 files is ethyl 2-aminopropanoate (ethyl alaninate): CH3CH2-O-C(=O)-CH(NH2)-CH3. Atom numbering is consistent across files (C1-C2 ethyl, O5 = ester O, C6 = carbonyl C, O7 = carbonyl O, C8 = alpha-CH, N9/H10/H11 = NH2, C12 = alpha-methyl). Two structural features dominate relative stability: (1) the ester group virtually always retains the low-energy Z (syn, C-O-C=O dihedral ~0°) conformation in every conformer (confirmed by spot-checks), so this is not a discriminator; (2) the amino group NH2 folds back to form an intramolecular N-H...O hydrogen bond, closing a 5-membered pseudo-ring through either the carbonyl oxygen (O7) or the ester (ether-type) oxygen (O5). Because the carbonyl oxygen carries more negative charge/better lone-pair availability than the resonance-donating ester oxygen, an N-H...O7 (carbonyl) interaction is intrinsically a stronger, more stabilizing H-bond than an N-H...O5 (ester-O) interaction of similar geometric distance.

By computing the shortest H10/H11...O7 and H10/H11...O5 distances in each conformer, all 30 structures fall into two families: Group A (short N-H...O7 contacts, 2.35-2.62 Å; true carbonyl-chelated conformers: 1,2,3,5,12,13,16,18,25,26,27,30) and Group B (long N-H...O7, >3.6 Å, but short N-H...O5 contacts, 2.35-2.52 Å; ester-oxygen-chelated conformers: 4,6,7,8,9,10,11,14,15,17,19,20,21,22,23,24,28,29). Group A is judged systematically more stable than Group B because the H-bond acceptor is the more basic carbonyl oxygen. Within each group, conformers are ranked by the tightness (shortness) of the relevant N-H...O contact as a proxy for hydrogen-bond strength/ring geometry quality (shorter = more linear/stronger interaction, all else being comparable). Ties within ~0.01 Å (e.g., 1 vs 13, 24 vs 29) are essentially indistinguishable from this geometric analysis and are broken arbitrarily; this is the main source of uncertainty. No severe steric clashes (very short non-bonded H...H or heavy-atom contacts) were found that would override this hydrogen-bond-based ordering, and the ethyl/methyl groups appear reasonably staggered in all conformers, so gauche/eclipsing effects are treated as a secondary, non-decisive factor.

This molecule is a vicinal diol: an isopropyl-substituted CH(OH) (C4) attached to a cyclopropane ring carbon that also bears an OH (C5). The cyclopropane ring strain and connectivity are identical in all conformers, so the dominant differentiator of relative stability is (1) whether the two OH groups can form an intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bond across the C4–C5 bond, and (2) how short/well-aligned that H-bond is. I extracted the two hydroxyl oxygens (on C4 and on the cyclopropane carbon C5) and their attached H atoms for every conformer and computed O···O distances and both possible H···O donor-acceptor distances (O-H(on C5)···O(on C4) and O-H(on C4)···O(on C5)).

A clear bimodal pattern emerged: about half the conformers have O···O distances of 2.66–2.97 Å with at least one H···O contact in the 2.0–2.5 Å range, consistent with a genuine (if sometimes weak-to-moderate) 5-membered-ring intramolecular hydrogen bond between the two OH groups. The other half have O···O distances of 3.5–3.7 Å and both H···O distances >3 Å, meaning the hydroxyls point away from each other with no intramolecular H-bond at all — these should be systematically less stable (loss of the main stabilizing interaction, no compensating intermolecular partner since this is an isolated molecule).

Within the H-bonded set, shorter/more linear H···O distances indicate stronger, more stabilizing interactions: conformer 28 (H···O ≈ 2.04 Å) and conformers 11/19 (≈2.14 Å) and 22 (≈2.19 Å) show the tightest, most favorable H-bond geometries. Conformers 20, 2, 1, 21, 9, 5, 8, 24 show moderate H-bonding (H···O ≈ 2.3–2.5 Å). Conformers 29, 14, 3, 26 show only weak/marginal H-bonding (H···O ≈ 2.45–2.7 Å, O···O closer to 3.0 Å), placing them near the boundary between bonded and non-bonded.

The non-hydrogen-bonded group (4, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 23, 25, 27, 30) all show O···O ~3.5–3.7 Å with no meaningful donor-acceptor contact; differences among them are small and likely reflect minor differences in isopropyl/cyclopropane torsional strain (gauche vs anti arrangements) rather than any H-bonding, so their relative order is uncertain and based only on small O···O distance differences as a weak tiebreaker.

Steric factors (isopropyl group clashing with cyclopropane CH2 hydrogens) were considered but are harder to quantify precisely from geometry alone; the H-bonding criterion is treated as the dominant, more chemically decisive factor, with steric/torsional details contributing secondary, more uncertain adjustments especially among conformers that are close in H-bond quality or lack an H-bond entirely.

The molecule (C7H15NO, ~24 atoms) is a tertiary amine consisting of an aziridine ring (N–C7–C8, a rigid 3-membered ring whose intrinsic strain is essentially conformation-independent) attached to a central stereocenter C5 that also bears an ethyl group (C2–C1) and a methoxymethyl arm (C13–O14–C15), plus one H. Since the aziridine ring strain itself cannot relax, the only source of relative-energy differences between conformers is rotation about the three flexible single bonds emanating from C5 (C5–C2, C5–N6, C5–C13) and the C13–O14/O14–C15 ether bonds, which determine gauche vs. anti relationships between the three bulky substituents (ethyl terminus C1, aziridine CH2's C7/C8, and the OMe terminus C15/O14).

To estimate steric strain without formal energy calculation, I measured a set of diagnostic 1,4-type non-bonded heavy-atom distances that report directly on these rotamer choices: d(C1–C7), d(C1–C8) [ethyl vs aziridine ring], d(C7–O14), d(C8–O14) [aziridine ring vs methoxymethyl oxygen], and d(C1–C15) [overall extension between the two chain termini]. Values near the 'anti' range (~3.8–5+ Å) indicate low steric penalty; values dropping toward ~3.0–3.3 Å indicate a gauche-type close contact (mild strain, few kcal/mol); values found were never below ~3.0 Å across any conformer (no severe eclipsing/clash was found after double-checking, including re-verifying an initially miscalculated short contact in conformer 28 which turned out to be only moderate, ~3.03 Å, not severe).

Based on this analysis:
- Conformers 14, 7, 20, 30, 21, 6, 25, 24, 4, 19 show no short (<3.3 Å) contacts among any of the diagnostic pairs — i.e., all three flexible dihedrals adopt favorable (mostly anti) arrangements, making them the most stable group, essentially isoenergetic within this crude metric (ranked by the size of their smallest contact distance).
- A larger group (18, 10, 1, 9, 27, 11, 8, 22, 15, 17, 5, 23, 2, 12, 3, 26, 28) each show exactly one moderate gauche-type contact (~3.0–3.55 Å) between one arm and another, corresponding to a single unfavorable rotamer choice (roughly one gauche-butane-like penalty), placing them as moderately stable/intermediate.
- Conformers 29, 13, and 16 show two such moderate short contacts simultaneously (double gauche penalty, e.g., aziridine ring gauche to both the ethyl and the OMe arm), making them the least favorable of the set.

No classical hydrogen-bond donor exists in this molecule (no O–H/N–H), so no strong intramolecular H-bonding differentiates conformers; only steric (gauche/anti) and mild dipole-alignment effects apply. Given the small magnitude of these effects (likely <2–3 kcal/mol spread total), the ranking—especially within the top 10 and within the large middle tier—carries meaningful uncertainty, and many of these conformers are likely very close in energy. The clearest, most confident calls are that 14/7/20/30 (very extended, no short contacts) are among the best, and 16/13/29 (double gauche clashes) are among the worst.

The molecule is a flexible C7 diol (HOCH2-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH(OH)-CH2-CH3, i.e. 3-methylhexane-1,4-diol type skeleton) with two OH groups separated by the C8-C12-C17-C18 backbone. The dominant stabilizing interaction available to this molecule is an intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond that closes a 6-membered ring (O-C-C-C-C-O + H). I measured the O...H distances between each hydroxyl H and the opposite oxygen in every conformer. Conformers cluster into three groups: (1) a 'strong' group with O...H distances of ~1.81-1.98 Å, consistent with a well-formed intramolecular H-bond stabilizing a folded/gauche backbone; (2) a 'moderate' group with O...H distances of ~2.27-2.40 Å, indicating a weaker, less optimally aligned H-bond (longer distance and/or poorer O-H...O angle); and (3) a group with no intramolecular H-bond (O...H > 3 Å), where the backbone is fully extended and the two OH groups point away from each other, losing the stabilizing interaction entirely (roughly 3-6 kcal/mol of stabilization typically lost for such intramolecular H-bonds).

Within the strong H-bond group, conformers with the shortest, most linear O-H...O contacts (≈1.81-1.86 Å) were ranked as most stable (8, 1, 13, 30, 16, 18, 28, 23, 20, 27, 11), followed by slightly longer but still strong H-bonds (10, 5, 6, 12, 19, 22, 25, ~1.87-1.98 Å). The moderate group (17, 26, 21, 24, ~2.27-2.40 Å) is next, since the H-bond is present but geometrically strained/elongated, providing less stabilization while still avoiding the fully extended penalty. Finally, the no-H-bond/extended conformers (2, 14, 29, 9, 15, 7, 3, 4) are ranked lowest, ordered internally by O...O separation as a rough proxy for how extended (anti, presumably lower gauche strain but no compensating H-bond) versus more folded-but-still-non-bonded they are — greater extension is assumed marginally more stable within this subgroup because it minimizes steric/gauche clashes even without the H-bond payoff.

Uncertainty: distinguishing conformers within the strong-H-bond cluster (differences of only 0.01-0.05 Å in H...O distance, plus unassessed subtle gauche/eclipsing differences in the ethyl and methyl substituents) is not highly reliable from geometry alone; likewise the internal ordering of the no-H-bond group is a weak heuristic. The three broad tiers (strong H-bond > moderate H-bond > no H-bond) are the most confident part of this ranking.

The molecule (C6H10O3) is a cyclopropane-1,2-diol bearing an acetonyl side chain (CH3-C(=O)-CH2- attached to one ring carbon that also carries an OH; the adjacent ring carbon carries the second OH; the third ring carbon is CH2). Atom indices are consistent across all files (1=CH3-C,2=carbonyl C,3=carbonyl O,4=CH2,7=quaternary ring C-OH(15/16),8=ring CH2,9=ring CH-OH(10/11)). Since the cyclopropane ring and its substituent stereochemistry are fixed, the only conformational degrees of freedom are rotations about the C7-C4, C4-C2 and C-O(H) bonds. The dominant stabilizing interaction available is an intramolecular O-H...O=C hydrogen bond between one of the two hydroxyls and the ketone oxygen (forming either a favorable 6-membered ring via the O15-H16 hydroxyl on the quaternary ring carbon, or a slightly larger 7-membered ring via the O10-H11 hydroxyl on the CH-OH ring carbon). I measured all four possible O(donor-H)...O(acceptor) distances (O15-H16→O3, O10-H11→O3, O15-H16→O10, O10-H11→O15) in every conformer.

Results: several conformers show a short, strong H-bond (O...H ≈ 1.87-2.14 Å): 26, 15, 5, 28, 13, 1, 21, 29, 3, 11, 6 — these should be the most stable, ranked internally by H-bond distance (shorter = stronger). A second tier shows only a moderate H-bond (2.2-2.6 Å): 22, 12, 20, 8, 24. A third tier shows only a weak long-range contact (2.6-3.0 Å): 17, 4, 18. The remaining conformers (9, 2, 30, 25, 19, 27, 10, 16, 7, 23, 14) show no meaningful O...H proximity (>3.0 Å, most >3.6 Å) — in these, the acetonyl chain and the two hydroxyls point away from each other, so no intramolecular H-bond stabilizes the structure; these are ranked lowest, with residual ordering based on the closest (still weak) O...H approach as a minor tie-breaker (this part of the ranking is low-confidence since differences are subtle rotamer effects only). No severe steric clashes (e.g. sub-2.0 Å non-bonded H...H or O...O repulsive contacts) were found that would override the hydrogen-bonding trend, and cyclopropane ring geometry (bond lengths/angles) is essentially invariant across conformers, so ring strain is not a differentiating factor here. Overall confidence is high for the top strongly H-bonded cluster and the bottom non-bonded cluster, but lower for fine ordering within the weak/none groups.

The molecule is a 2-ethyl-5-(hydroxymethyl)-2,5-dihydropyrrole (3-pyrroline) core: a 5-membered ring N10-C6-C7=C8-C9 (C7=C8 double bond, ~1.37-1.41 Å in all conformers, keeping that part of the ring nearly planar), with an ethyl substituent on C6 and a CH2OH substituent on C9, plus the ring N-H. Since all 30 files share identical connectivity, they represent the same diastereomer differing only in (a) rotation of the ethyl group about C6-C5, (b) rotation of the CH2OH group about C9-C12 and C12-O15, (c) O-H rotamer, and (d) slight envelope pucker of the ring.

The most chemically meaningful differentiator available from geometry is whether the hydroxyl oxygen (O15) and its H (H16) can approach the ring N10/N-H (H11) to form a stabilizing intramolecular electrostatic/H-bond-like contact (a 5-atom pseudo-ring N10-C9-C12-O15-H16...N10 or N10-H11...O15). I computed the N10···H16 and H11···O15 distances for every conformer as a proxy for this stabilization.

Most conformers show both distances in the 3.0-4.1 Å range, i.e. the hydroxymethyl arm points away from the amine and no significant attractive contact is formed. Two conformers stand out: #24 (H11···O15 = 2.41 Å) and #27 (H11···O15 = 2.41 Å), both with the CH2OH rotated so the oxygen lone pair sits close to the N-H hydrogen (bond angle ~95°, a bent but still attractive N-H···O contact at van-der-Waals-plus-electrostatic range). These two are therefore predicted to be extra-stabilized relative to the rest and are ranked highest.

Among the remaining 28 conformers, those with the next-shortest N/O-H proxy distances (~3.0-3.2 Å, e.g. 10, 5, 12, 29, 21, 11, 4, 25, 2) still have the CH2OH arm oriented somewhat toward the ring/N region, giving a weak residual stabilization, while conformers where both proxy distances exceed ~3.6-3.9 Å (9, 19, 13, 14, 22, 28, 20, 26) have the hydroxymethyl/OH rotated fully away from the ring nitrogen, losing any electrostatic stabilization and, in several of these (20, 26 especially), placing the terminal CH2OH gauche to the ethyl chain region, adding minor steric congestion.

Ring pucker and ethyl-group staggering appear to be secondary, smaller effects that are hard to resolve unambiguously from coordinates alone (no large bond-length or angle distortions were seen that would signal severe ring strain in any conformer), so the ranking within the middle cluster (roughly ranks 3-19) carries higher uncertainty and is based mainly on the magnitude of the N···H/O···H proxy distance, used as an indicator of favorable vs. unfavorable substituent rotamer placement. The bottom-ranked conformers (20, 26, 28, 14, 13, 22, 19, 9) consistently show the largest N/O separations, indicating the least favorable, most 'exposed' hydroxymethyl rotamer with no compensating intramolecular interaction.

The molecule (C7H10O2, HC≡C-CH2-C(CH3)(OH)-CH2-CHO) has a tertiary alcohol and an aldehyde separated by two CH2/one central C, plus a terminal alkyne arm. The dominant conformational driver is whether the hydroxyl H (H7) can form an intramolecular H-bond with the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen (O10), closing a favorable 5-membered pseudo-ring (O6-C5-C8-C9-O10...H7). I measured the H7···O10 distance and the O6-H7···O10 angle in every conformer:

- Conformers 30 (1.94 Å, 141°), 28 (2.07 Å, 132°), 17 (2.08 Å, 132°), 20 (2.11 Å, 130°), 23 (2.12 Å, 129°) and 10 (2.14 Å, 128°) all show a short H···O contact with a reasonable (though non-linear, ring-constrained) donor-H-acceptor angle, consistent with a genuine intramolecular O-H···O=C hydrogen bond. In all six the C9=O10 bond length (~1.20 Å) and O6-O10 separation (~2.8 Å) are consistent with a real H-bonded 5-ring, so these are judged the most stable set. Within this set, shorter H···O distance plus larger (more linear) angle is taken as better H-bonding quality, giving 30 > 28 ≈ 17 > 20 > 23 ≈ 10.

- A second group (13, 3, 16, 8) has intermediate H7···O10 distances (3.3–3.9 Å) but the O6-H7···O10 angle is far from linear (e.g. ~87° for 13), showing the OH is not actually pointing at the carbonyl — no true H-bond, only an accidental moderate approach. These are placed just below the H-bonded set: they may retain some favorable dipole alignment between the C-OH and C=O groups without full H-bond geometry, and lack the alkyne/aldehyde being forced into obviously clashing positions.

- The remaining 20 conformers show large H7···O10 separations (4.4–5.5 Å), i.e. the hydroxyl and carbonyl point away from each other with no compensating interaction; these are treated as lacking any stabilizing intramolecular interaction and are ranked lowest overall, ordered loosely by decreasing H7···O10 distance as a weak proxy for how far the polar groups (and their dipoles) are separated (more separated/extended conformations with dipoles that cannot align are assumed marginally less stabilized than the moderately folded ones, though these differences are expected to be small, <1–2 kcal/mol, and this part of the ranking is the most uncertain).

No severe steric clashes (sub-2.0 Å non-bonded H···H or O···H contacts) were found in the checked structures beyond normal 1,3-type contacts, so gross strain is not a major differentiator here; the ranking is driven mainly by presence/quality of the intramolecular H-bond, with the rest ordered by a weaker dipole/geometry heuristic and flagged as less certain.

The molecule is a tetrahydrofuran ring (ring atoms: ring-O9, C6, C3, C2, C10) bearing a methyl group on C2 and a 2-hydroxyethyl side chain (C10-C11H2-C13H2-O15H) on the ring carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. This topology allows the terminal hydroxyl (O15-H16) to fold back and form an intramolecular O-H...O(ring) hydrogen bond through a favorable 6-membered pseudo-ring (O9-C10-C11-C13-O15-H16...O9). This H-bond is the dominant differentiator of conformer stability, since all conformers share the same connectivity/ring strain baseline and no other strong polar contacts (e.g., no amide/large dipole clashes) are present.

I measured the O9(ring ether)···H16(hydroxyl H) distance and the O9···O15 distance in every conformer. Six conformers (3, 12, 5, 23, 17, 14) show O9···H16 distances of ~1.97-2.10 Å and O9···O15 distances of ~2.77-2.82 Å, both fully consistent with a genuine, well-formed intramolecular hydrogen bond. These are essentially tied in quality (differences <0.13 Å, within conformational noise), so they are ranked as the most stable group, ordered by slightly shorter H···O distance (3 < 12 < 5 < 23 < 17 < 14).

Conformer 27 shows an intermediate, weaker H-bond (H···O ~2.58 Å, O···O ~3.16 Å) — geometrically plausible but less optimal (longer, likely less linear), so it is placed next.

Conformers 2, 11, 13, and 1 show intermediate H···O distances (3.2–4.0 Å) that are too long for a real hydrogen bond but indicate the chain is still partially folded toward the ring oxygen, giving some residual electrostatic/dipole stabilization relative to fully extended conformers.

The remaining conformers (22, 6, 26, 25, 7, 20, 21, 29, 28, 19, 4, 24, 10, 16, 9, 15, 18, 8, 30) all have the hydroxyl chain pointed away from the ring oxygen (H···O > 4.1 Å, up to 4.9 Å), meaning no intramolecular H-bond stabilization is present; these are ranked as least stable, ordered by increasing H···O distance as a weak secondary indicator of how far the polar groups are from any favorable alignment (acknowledging that within this tail group the differences are small and could also be influenced by minor steric/torsional effects not captured by this single metric — so the exact internal order here carries higher uncertainty).

No severe steric clashes (close nonbonded heavy-atom or H···H contacts <2.0 Å) were found that would override this hydrogen-bonding-based ranking in the top group; methyl-group proximity to the hydroxyethyl chain was checked in the top six and found not to cause any clash (closest contacts >3 Å). Overall confidence is high for the separation between H-bonded (top 7) and non-H-bonded (bottom 23) conformers, but lower for fine ordering within the non-bonded tail.

The molecule (CH3-CH(CHO)-CH2-O-CH=NH, a branched aldehyde bearing a formimidate-ether side chain) has three flexible C-C/C-O bonds plus a formimidate N-H that can act as a weak intramolecular H-bond donor toward the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen. Because the two polar groups (the aldehyde C=O and the formimidate N-H) are the strongest local dipoles in the molecule, I used the through-space distance between the amine/imine N-H proton (atom 15) and the aldehyde oxygen (atom 7) as the principal geometric proxy for stabilizing electrostatic/H-bond-like interaction: conformers that fold the chain so this N-H sits closer to the carbonyl oxygen benefit from favorable dipole alignment and possible weak N-H...O=C contact, while fully extended/anti conformers that place these groups far apart (5.5-6.8 Å) lose this stabilization and are more likely to be simple extended rotamers with less favorable dipole cancellation. I computed this N-H(15)-O(7) distance for all 30 conformers. Two conformers (29 and 12) show the shortest distances (~2.83 Å), consistent with a favorable folded geometry bringing the two dipolar groups close without introducing obvious van der Waals clashes (checked surrounding atom-atom distances in these two structures; no contacts under ~2.3 Å that would indicate serious steric strain). Conformers 30 and 20 (~3.2 Å) are next-most compact. Conformers such as 18, 2, and 6 show intermediate folding (3.8-4.2 Å). The majority of conformers (9, 21, 5, 23, 17, 28, 25, 22, 14, 10, 27, 4, 13, 15, 16, 11, 8, 7) show extended, largely anti backbone conformations with the two polar termini pointing away from each other (5-6.6 Å), which are treated as roughly similar in stability, differing mainly in minor gauche/anti choices at the C-C and C-O bonds that are harder to resolve without full force-field energies. Conformers 19, 26, 3, and 1 show the largest separations (6.7-6.9 Å) between the N-H and carbonyl O, suggesting the least favorable relative orientation of the two dipoles and are placed as least stable. This ranking is inherently approximate: differences between conformers in the middle of the list (roughly ranks 9-25) are subtle and could reorder with a full force-field or QM single-point evaluation, since factors like exact torsion strain, C-H...O contacts, and eclipsing interactions along the CH3-CH-CH2-O backbone were not exhaustively enumerated. The clearest, most confident calls are the top few (29, 12, 30, 20) showing genuine folding toward an intramolecular dipole-stabilized geometry, and the bottom few (1, 3, 26, 19) showing the most extended, dipole-unfavorable arrangement.

Intermediate anti-leaning conformers (160-170°, e.g., 2, 3, 7, 13, 15, 16, 23, 25, 30) fall in the middle, as do a few gauche conformers biased toward the steeper (cis-like, <95°) side (6, 20, 29, 19) which incur a somewhat larger penalty per degree of deviation than their anti counterparts of similar |Δ|.

No severe extra steric clashes (very short non-bonded H···H/H···O contacts) were found that would override this ranking in an obvious way, though such second-order effects (allylic eclipsing at the C2-C4 and C5-C6 single bonds, methyl rotor orientation) were not exhaustively quantified and add uncertainty, especially among conformers with similar peroxide-torsion penalties (e.g., the many structures clustered near 150-180°). The overall ranking should therefore be treated as most confident at the extremes (best few and worst few) and least confident for the closely bunched middle group.
